title: Empty the tanks into the backwardation
trade: Sell 1 Mbbl of WTI from Cushing tanks on the December contract, buy the February contract to refill
why: WTI is backwardated by about 1.2 $/bbl a month, so the market pays to release barrels now.
Both export arbs are shut. WTI lands in Rotterdam and in Ningbo above the local alternative, so the barrel is worth more sold at home.
Hormuz has been shut since March, which keeps the front of the curve tight. PortWatch counted 27 transits in the week to 8 November, against 527 a year earlier.
US crude stocks rose 9 Mbbl in the week to 6 November (API), so the refill should not be short.
hedge: The February futures are the refill. They are swapped for physical (EFP) when the barrels come back.
risks: The tank is empty for two months. If a customer or a blend needs the barrels in January, they are bought back at the prompt price.
Cushing physical trades over futures at the refill.
The tank rent runs whether the tank is full or not.

good.case: refill at a discount after more stock builds

bad.case: barrels needed in January, bought back in a squeeze 3.5 $/bbl over February

title: Sell diesel prompt, buy it back in February
trade: Sell 37 kt of ULSD from New York Harbor tanks on the December contract, buy February NYMEX ULSD to refill
why: The distillate curve is the steepest on the board, about 2% a month in New York Harbor.
ICE gasoil for November expired 91 $/t over December on 12 November. Prompt barrels are short on both sides of the Atlantic.
No cargo pays across the Atlantic in either direction once freight and RINs are counted, so the tank is the outlet.
Russian refining is down about 30% since late October after drone strikes.
hedge: The February NYMEX ULSD futures are the refill, swapped for physical by EFP.
risks: A cold January pulls heating oil demand forward and the barrels are bought back early, at the prompt price.
New York barges trade over futures at the refill.

good.case: refill at a discount as imports arrive

bad.case: bought back early in a squeeze the size of November gasoil's, 91 $/t over the next month

title: A mid-December US cargo pays more in Asia than in Europe
trade: Buy a FOB Sabine Pass cargo at its European netback, sell DES Japan or Korea on JKM for the day it lands
laycan: Load around 12 December, land in the first days of January
why: A spot US cargo is priced off Europe, its usual outlet. 57% of US exports went there in September.
For mid-December, JKM is about 1.5 $/MMBtu over TTF. Japan through Panama costs about 0.65 more to reach than Rotterdam.
JKM is backwardated, with January 0.87 below December. A cargo landing on 3 January is priced between the two, which takes about 0.5 off.
hedge: At loading, sell JKM and buy TTF for the landing month, for the cargo size.
risks: No Panama slot. Round the Cape the voyage takes two weeks more and the cargo would have been better off in Europe.
Sold DES, the boil-off and any delay are the seller's.
A cold spell in Europe closes the gap before the hedge is on.

good.case: JKM − TTF widens by 1 on Asian tenders before the hedge is on

bad.case: no Panama slot, the cargo goes round the Cape

title: South African coal goes east, not to Europe
trade: Buy 150 kt FOB Richards Bay on API4, sell CFR Japan at Newcastle plus freight, less a quality discount
laycan: Load around 12 December, land in early January
why: Europe is shut. API2 − API4 is about 11 $/t against 24 $/t of Capesize freight to Rotterdam.
Japan pays Newcastle plus the Panamax freight from Australia. Sold 5 $/t under that, a Capesize from Richards Bay still clears its costs.
API4 is backwardated, 128.6 for November against 126.6 for December, so a December cargo is bought cheaper.
hedge: Buy API4 swaps against the purchase and sell NEWC swaps against the sale. Fix the Capesize the day the cargo is bought.
risks: The discount is the trade. Japanese boilers are tuned to Australian coal, and a utility that does not need the cargo asks 10 $/t.
Coal that Transnet has not railed keeps the ship waiting off Richards Bay. The claim against the supplier is paid late and at the contract rate.
Until the ship is fixed, each +10k $/day on the Capesize costs about 3.9 $/t.

bad.case: the buyer asks 10 $/t and the ship waits two weeks off Richards Bay

title: European coil still lands under US prices after the tariff
trade: Buy 30 kt of coil ex-works in the Ruhr, sell duty paid in Houston on the CME price of the landing month
laycan: Ship around 12 December, land at the end of the month
why: US Midwest coil is 1,401 $/st for December, about 1,545 $/t. European coil costs 853 $/t at the mill, then 30 to reach the ship, 45 of freight and 442 of tariff.
The EU's steel regime, with a 50% out-of-quota duty since 1 July, shut Chinese coil out of Europe. European mills have tonnes to place.
The CME curve is in contango, with January at 1,430 $/st, so a sale priced on landing pays more than today.
hedge: Sell CME HRC futures for the landing month when the purchase is fixed. They cover the US price, not the discount an import sells at.
risks: Unhedged, a fall in US prices before the cargo lands comes straight out of the margin.
Sold duty paid, the tariff is the seller's. A rate change before customs clearance hits the margin.
A US anti-dumping case on European flat steel.

good.case: the buyer takes it 40 $/t closer to domestic coil

bad.case: unhedged, US coil falls 150 $/st before the cargo lands

title: Copper into the US before a tariff, an option the curve already prices
trade: Take 5 kt of copper out of an LME warehouse in Rotterdam, land it in Baltimore before 1 January and hold it against COMEX
laycan: Ship by 12 December, land before the year ends
why: Commerce recommended 15% on refined copper from 1 January 2027. The White House has not decided.
COMEX is only about 25 $/t over the LME for December, but about 300 $/t over for March. On a 15% tariff worth 2,000 $/t, the curve gives it roughly one chance in seven.
Landing metal before the deadline costs about 135 $/t more than the December spread pays back. That is the price of the option.
hedge: Buy LME December and sell LME March against the metal, so only the US premium stays open. Selling COMEX March instead locks about 300 $/t and gives the option away.
risks: No tariff. The March spread falls back to where December is and three months of carry are lost.
The metal must clear customs before the tariff starts, or the duty lands on the trader.
A queue at the LME warehouse in Rotterdam delays the load-out past the deadline.

bad.case: no tariff, and the metal is carried to March for nothing
